title: Check yourself: finding and fixing visibility bugs

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: An order-matching thread runs `while (!halted) { matchNext(); }`, where `halted` is a plain boolean field that an admin thread sets. In production the thread now and then keeps matching after a halt. A developer runs the service for a day with `-Xint`, then for a day with the loop's method excluded from compilation, and the halt works every time in both. What should they conclude?

options.text: The compiled loop reads `halted` once and loops on that value, since no edge orders the admin thread's write before the loop's reads
options.says: the switches only change which code runs; C2 may hoist a plain read because no happens-before edge leads from the write to it, so the fix is an edge

options.text: The compiled loop reads `halted` wrongly because of a JIT bug, since compiled and interpreted code must run a program the same way
options.says: the memory model allows the compiled loop to read the plain field once; the interpreter reading it every turn is a choice, not a promise

options.text: The halt needs the admin thread's core to flush its cache, since a plain write to `halted` reaches other cores only after a flush
options.says: the hardware keeps caches coherent; the interpreter on the same hardware sees the write, so the stale value is the compiled code's

options.text: The halt needs the loop's method kept out of the JIT, since interpreted code reads `halted` on every turn
options.says: a run with the method excluded proves nothing about the production JVM; the fix is an edge such as volatile, a lock or an atomic class

origin.section: A Visibility Bug Disappears Under -Xint, C1, a Breakpoint or a Log Line: That Is the Diagnosis, Not a Fix

questions.stem: An inventory service keeps `volatile Catalog catalog`, and `Catalog` holds a plain `HashMap<String, Integer> prices`. A pricing job runs `catalog.prices.put("sku-9", 1299)`. Checkout threads run `catalog.prices.get("sku-9")` on every request. What does the memory model promise the checkout threads?

options.text: They are promised the new price on their next request, since each of them reads the volatile `catalog` field before it reads the map
options.says: a volatile read publishes nothing by itself; only a volatile write orders the writes before it, and the job makes none

options.text: They are promised the new price once the job then writes a volatile `lastPricedAt` field, since a volatile write publishes every earlier write to all threads
options.says: a volatile write publishes only to a reader that reads that same field and sees the value; the checkout threads never read lastPricedAt

options.text: They are not promised the new price, since the job's `put` reads the volatile `catalog` field but never writes it
options.says: the put is a volatile read of catalog followed by plain writes inside the map; replacing the Catalog would be the volatile write that publishes

options.text: They are not promised the new price, since each checkout thread keeps its own cached copy of the volatile `catalog` field
options.says: no cache hides a write, since caches are coherent, and each checkout reads catalog afresh; the gap is that the job never writes catalog, only plain fields inside the map

origin.section: volatile Covers Reads of the Field, Not the Object It Points To

questions.stem: A rate limiter keeps one switch per tenant in `private volatile int[] throttled`. A control thread runs `throttled[7] = 1`. Tenant 7's worker runs `drain(throttled, 7)`, where `drain(int[] t, int tenant)` loops `while (t[tenant] == 0) { serveNext(); }`. What does the memory model promise about the worker?

options.text: It is not guaranteed to stop, since the control thread's element write and the worker's element reads are plain accesses
options.says: volatile covers the field holding the array reference; t[tenant] reads an element through a plain parameter, with no edge from the control thread's element write

options.text: It is not guaranteed to stop, since an array passed as a parameter is copied when the call starts
options.says: Java passes the reference, not a copy of the array; the problem is that element accesses are plain

options.text: It is guaranteed to stop at its next check, since the elements of an array held in a volatile field are volatile too
options.says: a volatile array gives its elements no edge; AtomicIntegerArray or a VarHandle on every access does

options.text: It is guaranteed to stop at its next check, since writing an element also writes the volatile field holding the array
options.says: throttled[7] = 1 reads the field and writes the element; the field itself is never written

origin.section: A volatile Array Gives Its Elements No Edge: Use AtomicIntegerArray or a VarHandle

questions.stem: A feature-flag client publishes each poll's flags as a new `Flags` record in a volatile field. At 09:00 a report job runs `Flags f = client.flags()` and then calls `f.enabled("new-tax-rules")` before each of its 40,000 invoices, which take two hours. At 09:30 the flag is turned off and the next poll publishes new flags. Which flag value do the invoices after 09:30 use?

options.text: The value from 09:00, since the poll's write reaches threads that start after it, and the thread holding `f` started before
options.says: a thread that reads the volatile field after the write sees the new record, whenever it started; the once-per-charge worker was running before the pause and saw it

options.text: The value from 09:00, since `f` goes on pointing to the record it was given, whatever the field holds later
options.says: f keeps the record client.flags() returned at 09:00; a snapshot reaches a reader only when it reads the field again

options.text: The new value, since a volatile write of a new record also changes the record that `f` points to
options.says: the volatile write puts a new record in the field; the record the job already holds is a different object and doesn't change

options.text: The new value, since each call to `enabled` through `f` reads the volatile field again
options.says: f is a local copy of the reference; calls through it never touch the volatile field, so they keep asking the 09:00 record

origin.section: Settings Are One Immutable Snapshot, Replaced Whole and Read Once per Unit of Work

concepts: volatile on an array field covers the reference only; element writes are plain, and an array passed as a parameter is read with plain accesses.

-Xint, C1 only, excluding the method from compilation, a breakpoint in it or a log line in the loop each make a hoisted plain read go away by changing which code runs, not what the memory model allows; the hang is evidence for the diagnosis and the fix is a happens-before edge.
A change made to an object reached through a volatile field is a volatile read followed by a plain write, so no reader is guaranteed to see it.
